Chapter 8—The Power of Imagination: Dreaming Beyond the Present.
Have you ever noticed how tough it can be to imagine a world that’s completely different from the one we live in right now? With our routines, the weight of everything that’s come before, and all those voices telling us what’s “realistic,” it’s easy to feel boxed in. But honestly, every push for justice starts with someone daring to imagine something better—someone refusing to accept that this is all there is.
Picture this: a teenager, tired of the violence in her neighborhood, begins to ask herself—what if safety didn’t have to mean police on every corner? Or a group of friends, each of them heartbroken over loved ones behind bars, start to dream about a world without prisons. Sure, at first, those dreams feel wild—maybe even impossible. But those are the seeds that can grow into real change.
This chapter invites you to stretch your imagination even further. Instead of just tweaking what’s already there, what if you asked, “What would it actually mean to abolish systems of oppression?” Most of us don’t even realize how much our sense of what’s possible is shaped by the world as it is. The idea of abolition—getting rid of prisons, police, even borders—can seem radical, maybe even a little scary. But think about this: every huge shift in history once felt unthinkable.
Imagination isn’t just about daydreams or fantasy. It’s about having the courage to ask tough questions and not settling for halfway fixes. What if, instead of pouring money into punishment, we invested in our communities? What if schools were places for healing, not just control? Imagine if borders could connect us, instead of dividing us.
For a lot of people, dreaming up something completely new is both thrilling and a little terrifying. It means letting go of what we’ve always known, being willing to stumble, and trusting in the creativity of everyone around us. But here’s the beautiful part—it also means unlocking new hope and discovering possibilities in the most unexpected places.
The author brings to life stories of communities already building these alternatives—think restorative justice circles, community gardens, mutual aid networks. No, these experiments aren’t perfect. But they give us a glimpse of what’s possible. Most folks might walk right past these small acts of creation. Still, they’re laying the foundation for a future that looks completely different—and maybe, just maybe, a whole lot brighter.
